words.definition: Plain and severe, with no comfort, decoration, or indulgence.
words.example: The monk's austere room held only a wooden cot, a candle, and a single book.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'oh, stern' — an austere teacher is stern and offers no frills.

words.definition: Boldly disrespectful, acting without any shame or embarrassment.
words.example: In a brazen move, she walked past the guards and took the file off his desk.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'brass' — a person made of brass is hard and shameless, showing bold cheek.

words.definition: Honest and direct, saying exactly what one thinks.
words.example: When I asked for his real opinion, he was candid: the plan would fail.
words.mnemonic: A 'candid camera' catches you unposed and real — candid means open and unguarded.

words.definition: Rude and bad-tempered, lacking courtesy toward others.
words.example: It seemed churlish to refuse the gift after they had driven so far to bring it.
words.mnemonic: A 'churl' was a low-born peasant; churlish = behaving with surly, ill-mannered gruffness.

words.definition: Shy and lacking confidence in one's own abilities.
words.example: Too diffident to raise his hand, he knew the answer but stayed silent.
words.mnemonic: 'Dif-' (not) + 'fident' (from confident) — a diffident person is simply not confident.

words.definition: Refusing to give up despite difficulty or opposition.
words.example: Her dogged pursuit of the truth kept her digging long after everyone else quit.
words.mnemonic: Like a dog with a bone that won't let go — dogged means stubbornly persistent.

words.definition: Very attentive to detail and hard to please about cleanliness or quality.
words.example: A fastidious cook, he wiped every counter and measured each grain of salt.
words.mnemonic: 'Fast-tidy-us' — someone who keeps things tidy fast and to an exacting standard.

words.definition: Talking too much, especially about trivial things.
words.example: The garrulous passenger narrated his entire life story before we left the runway.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'gargle' — a garrulous person gargles out an endless stream of words.

words.definition: Behaving as if superior to others; arrogantly proud.
words.example: She gave the waiter a haughty look and refused to say thank you.
words.mnemonic: 'Haughty' hides 'high' (from French 'haut') — you hold your nose high above everyone.

words.definition: Acting quickly on impulse without thinking of the consequences.
words.example: In an impetuous instant he quit his job and booked a one-way flight abroad.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'impetus' (a sudden push) — an impetuous act is pushed by impulse.

words.definition: Wanting to avoid effort; habitually lazy.
words.example: The indolent cat spent the whole afternoon sprawled in the one warm patch of sun.
words.mnemonic: 'In-' (not) + 'dolent' (from Latin for pain/effort) — taking no pains, avoiding all work.

words.definition: Rude and disrespectful, showing open contempt for authority.
words.example: The insolent recruit rolled his eyes as the sergeant gave an order.
words.mnemonic: An 'insolent' teen shows no respect — think 'in-your-face' plus a sneering tone.

words.definition: Cheerful and friendly, full of good humor.
words.example: The jovial host kept everyone laughing with one warm joke after another.
words.mnemonic: From 'Jove' (Jupiter); those born under Jupiter were thought merry — jovial means jolly.

words.definition: Using very few words to express something.
words.example: Asked how the mission went, the soldier gave a laconic reply: "Done."
words.mnemonic: The ancient people of Laconia (Sparta) were famous for terse, clipped speech.

words.definition: Generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or weaker person.
words.example: In victory she was magnanimous, praising the team she had just beaten.
words.mnemonic: 'Magna' (great) + 'animus' (spirit) — a magnanimous person has a great, big-hearted spirit.

words.definition: Showing extreme care about small details and doing things precisely.
words.example: She kept meticulous records, logging every expense down to the last cent.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'met-a-tick' — picture counting every single tick on a clock, one by one.

words.definition: Trying too hard to please by excessive flattery and eager obedience.
words.example: The obsequious waiter kept bowing and praising every choice the diners made.
words.mnemonic: Say 'ob-SEEK-we-us' — someone always seeking to please you.

words.definition: Displayed in a flashy way designed to impress and attract attention.
words.example: His ostentatious gold watch and neon sports car announced his wealth to the whole street.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'ostent' ≈ 'on stage' — always showing off on stage.

words.definition: Sulky and irritable, like a spoiled child in a small tantrum.
words.example: He gave a petulant shrug and refused to answer any more questions.
words.mnemonic: 'PET-you-lant' — imagine a pampered pet pouting when it doesn't get its way.

words.definition: Handling problems in a practical, sensible way instead of an idealistic one.
words.example: Rather than chase grand dreams, she took a pragmatic route and fixed what was already broken.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'pragma' (deed/action) — it shares 'pra-' with 'practical.'

words.definition: Reluctant to share one's thoughts or feelings; reserved in speech.
words.example: He was reticent about his past, changing the subject whenever it came up.
words.mnemonic: 'Reti-CENT' — he holds onto every cent and every word, giving nothing away.

words.definition: Mocking or scornful in a bitter, cynical manner.
words.example: 'Wonderful,' she muttered with a sardonic smile as the engine died again.
words.mnemonic: Starts like 'sarcastic' (sar-); legend says a Sardinian plant twisted the face into a bitter grin.

words.definition: Very careful to act honestly and get every detail exactly right.
words.example: The scrupulous accountant double-checked each figure to avoid the smallest mistake.
words.mnemonic: Full of 'scruples'; Latin 'scrupulus' was a tiny sharp stone — like a pebble in your shoe nagging your conscience.

words.definition: Serious, settled, and rather dull in a respectable, unadventurous way.
words.example: The staid old bank hadn't changed its dark wood interior in fifty years.
words.mnemonic: Sounds exactly like 'stayed' — someone who stayed put and never changes.

words.definition: Naturally saying very little; habitually silent.
words.example: The taciturn farmer answered every question with a single grunted word.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'tacitus' (silent) — same root as 'tacit,' an unspoken agreement.

words.definition: Aggressively defiant and eager to argue or fight.
words.example: The truculent teenager glared around the room, daring anyone to correct him.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'truck' — picture a truck barreling straight at you, spoiling for a crash.

words.definition: Polished, sophisticated, and smoothly courteous in social situations.
words.example: The urbane host drifted through the party, charming every guest with easy wit.
words.mnemonic: Almost 'urban' — think of the polished, cultured manners of a worldly city dweller.

words.definition: Strongly wanting to harm someone who has wronged you; spiteful.
words.example: After the breakup she grew vindictive, spreading lies to wreck his reputation.
words.mnemonic: Root 'vindicta' (revenge) — the same idea powers 'vendetta.'

words.definition: Full of energetic, passionate commitment to a cause or goal.
words.example: The zealous volunteers knocked on every door in the neighborhood twice.
words.mnemonic: Built from 'zeal' — burning enthusiasm; hear the fiery 'zee' at the front.

words.definition: Warm, friendly, and easy to talk to.
words.example: Our affable neighbor greeted everyone with a smile and a joke over the fence.
words.mnemonic: 'A-FAB-le' — a fabulously friendly person; Latin 'affari' means 'to speak to.'

words.definition: Keeping emotionally or physically distant; unfriendly and unwilling to engage with others.
words.example: The new manager stayed aloof at the party, standing by the window instead of mingling with the team.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a-roof' — picture someone sitting alone up on a roof, far above and apart from everyone below.

words.definition: Caring more about helping others than about personal gain or reward.
words.example: Her altruistic decision to donate a kidney to a stranger stunned everyone who knew her.
words.mnemonic: 'Altruistic' hides 'all true' — a truly good person who puts all others first.

words.definition: Having a pleasant, good-natured manner that makes people feel at ease.
words.example: Our amiable host greeted each guest with a warm smile and remembered every name.
words.mnemonic: 'Ami' is French for 'friend' — an amiable person is easy to be friends with.

words.definition: Eager to fight or argue; showing an aggressive, hostile attitude.
words.example: The belligerent customer slammed his fist on the counter and demanded a refund at the top of his voice.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'belli' from Latin 'bellum' (war) — a belligerent person is always ready for war.

words.definition: Rude and clumsy in behavior, with no regard for good manners.
words.example: His boorish habit of chewing loudly and interrupting made dinner unbearable for the other guests.
words.mnemonic: A 'boor' plus 'ish' — picture a wild boar crashing through a fancy party, knocking things over.

words.definition: Showing no sympathy for the suffering of other people.
words.example: The landlord's callous reply to the flooded tenants was simply, "Pay the rent or leave."
words.mnemonic: A callus is hardened skin — a callous person has a hardened heart that feels nothing.

words.definition: Changing suddenly and unpredictably, often for no clear reason.
words.example: The capricious weather turned from bright sunshine to hail within a single afternoon.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a-price-is' — a shop whose prices change on a whim every time you visit.

words.definition: Careful to consider all consequences before acting or speaking.
words.example: A circumspect investor, she read every clause twice before signing anything.
words.mnemonic: 'Circum' (around) + 'spect' (look) — you look all around you before you take a step.

words.definition: Intended to calm anger and win back goodwill after a disagreement.
words.example: He sent a conciliatory email apologizing for the mix-up and offering a full refund.
words.mnemonic: Related to 'reconcile' — a conciliatory gesture brings two sides back together.

words.definition: Likely to cause disagreement or argument; eager to quarrel.
words.example: The contentious topic of the budget split the committee into two shouting camps.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'contention' inside it — a contentious issue is full of contention and dispute.

words.definition: Warm and friendly in a sincere, welcoming way.
words.example: Despite their rivalry, the two candidates shared a cordial handshake before the debate.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'cor' (heart) — a cordial greeting comes straight from the heart.

words.definition: Lacking any courage; shamefully afraid.
words.example: In a craven move, the officer abandoned his post the moment danger appeared.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'crave-in' — a coward who caves in and craves any way out of a fight.

words.definition: Believing that people act only out of selfishness, not good intentions.
words.example: After years in politics, she grew cynical and assumed every promise hid a hidden motive.
words.mnemonic: A cynic sees a 'sick-ical' world — always sickened by others' supposed selfishness.

words.definition: Showing great respect by yielding to another person's wishes or authority.
words.example: The young intern was so deferential that she never spoke until the senior partners had finished.
words.mnemonic: To 'defer' to someone is to give way — a deferential person always defers to their elders.

words.definition: Quick and skillful in movement or handling of a situation.
words.example: With a few deft strokes of the knife, the chef diced the onion in seconds.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'left' but think of a magician's swift hands — 'deft' fingers move like lightning.

words.definition: Feeling deep sadness and loss of hope, with no expectation things will improve.
words.example: After his third rejection letter in a week, he sat by the window, despondent, unable to imagine trying again.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'de-SPOND' — your spirit stops responding, no more 'spond' left in you.

words.definition: Showing careful, steady, and persistent effort in one's work or duties.
words.example: The diligent intern double-checked every figure before submitting the report, never leaving a single cell unverified.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'dig it': a diligent worker keeps digging in until the job is truly done.

words.definition: Showing contempt or scorn because you think someone or something is unworthy.
words.example: She gave the cheap knockoff a disdainful glance and set it back on the shelf without a word.
words.mnemonic: 'This ain't full' of worth — a disdainful sneer says something is beneath you.

words.definition: Stern, gloomy, and unfriendly in manner or appearance.
words.example: The dour old caretaker never smiled, greeting each visitor with a silent, grim stare.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'sour' — a dour face looks as sour as a lemon.

words.definition: Sincere and seriously committed, without joking or pretense.
words.example: In an earnest voice, the boy promised to repay every cent, and you could tell he meant it.
words.mnemonic: 'Earn-est' — someone who truly wants to earn your trust means what they say.

words.definition: Expressing feelings, especially gratitude or praise, in an unrestrained and gushing way.
words.example: He was so effusive in his thanks that he hugged every guest twice and nearly cried.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'effusus' (poured out) — an effusive person pours out emotion like water.

words.definition: Excessively concerned with oneself and one's own importance; conceited.
words.example: The egotistical actor spent the whole interview talking about himself and never once asked about anyone else.
words.mnemonic: 'Ego' at the center — an egotistical person makes their ego the whole story.

words.definition: Having or showing intense, passionate feeling about something.
words.example: A fervent supporter of the team, she painted her face and cheered until her voice gave out.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'fervere' = to boil (same root as 'fever') — fervent feelings run hot.

words.definition: Treating a serious matter with inappropriate lightness or a lack of respect.
words.example: When the judge asked if he understood the charges, his flippant 'sure, whatever' made things worse.
words.mnemonic: 'Flip' — a flippant person flips off serious things with a careless joke.

words.definition: Careful and sparing with money or resources; avoiding waste.
words.example: Being frugal, she packed her lunch every day and repaired her shoes rather than buying new ones.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'few gal(lons)' — a frugal driver uses as few gallons as possible.

words.definition: Fond of the company of others; sociable and outgoing.
words.example: So gregarious was the new hire that she had made friends with half the office by lunchtime.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'grex' (herd) — a gregarious person loves being in the herd.

words.definition: Innocent and honest, without any cunning or intent to deceive.
words.example: Her guileless answer revealed the surprise party, since it never occurred to her to lie.
words.mnemonic: 'Guile' (trickery) + 'less' — guileless means with no trickery at all.

words.definition: Determined to do things one's own way, refusing others' advice or direction.
words.example: The headstrong toddler insisted on tying his own shoes and howled when anyone tried to help.
words.mnemonic: A 'strong head' that won't turn — a headstrong person won't bend their mind for anyone.

words.definition: Having a modest view of one's own importance; not proud or arrogant.
words.example: Even after winning the prize, she stayed humble and credited her whole team for the success.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'humus' (ground) — a humble person keeps their feet on the ground.

words.definition: Commanding others in an arrogant, domineering way that expects instant obedience.
words.example: With an imperious wave of her hand, the duchess dismissed the servants before they could speak.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'imperi-' as in emperor/empire — an imperious person acts like a bossy emperor.

words.definition: Boldly rude or disrespectful, showing no proper regard for others.
words.example: The impudent student rolled his eyes and told the teacher her lesson was a waste of time.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'imp' with no 'prudence' — a cheeky little devil who won't behave.

words.definition: Showing sharp, clear thinking that cuts straight to the heart of a matter.
words.example: Her incisive questions exposed the flaw in the argument within seconds.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'incision' and 'scissors' — it cuts cleanly through.

words.definition: Working hard and steadily with great effort and diligence.
words.example: The industrious intern arrived early every day and finished twice the assigned work.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'industry' — picture busy factories humming with constant work.

words.definition: Innocent and trusting, showing a childlike honesty and lack of guile.
words.example: Her ingenuous smile made it clear she suspected nothing of the surprise being planned.
words.mnemonic: The 'gen' root means 'born' — as open and pure as a newborn. Don't confuse with 'ingenious' (clever).

words.definition: Fearless and brave, especially when facing danger or difficulty.
words.example: The intrepid explorer pressed on into the storm while the others turned back.
words.mnemonic: 'In' (not) + Latin 'trepidus' (trembling) — one who does not tremble.

words.definition: Easily made angry; quick to lose one's temper.
words.example: The irascible old man shouted at anyone who dared step on his lawn.
words.mnemonic: Starts like 'ire' (anger) — an 'ire-ascible' person boils over fast.

words.definition: Worn out or bored, having lost enthusiasm through too much of something.
words.example: After twenty years reviewing films, the critic felt jaded and could no longer be surprised.
words.mnemonic: Picture a cold 'jade' statue — beautiful but lifeless, dulled by time.

words.definition: Having a lively, cheerful, and confident manner.
words.example: He walked in with a jaunty tip of his hat and a spring in his step.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'jaunt' (a fun little outing) — the cheerful bounce of someone off on a lark.

words.definition: Showing good sense and careful thought in making decisions.
words.example: A judicious use of the budget left the team with savings for emergencies.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'judge' and 'judgment' — a good judge decides wisely.

words.definition: Tending to talk a great deal; very chatty.
words.example: Our loquacious guide barely paused for breath during the entire three-hour tour.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'loqui' (to speak) — same root as 'eloquent' and 'soliloquy.'

words.definition: Looking or sounding sad and gloomy, often in an exaggerated way.
words.example: The hound gave a lugubrious howl and slumped by the door as if the world were ending.
words.mnemonic: The slow, dragging 'loo-goo-brious' sound feels heavy and mournful just to say.

words.definition: Changing moods quickly and unpredictably.
words.example: Her mercurial temper meant we never knew if she'd greet us with a laugh or a scowl.
words.mnemonic: From Mercury — the fast-moving planet and the liquid metal that darts around when touched.

words.definition: Not boastful about one's abilities; humble and unassuming.
words.example: Despite winning the prize, she gave a modest shrug and credited her whole team.
words.mnemonic: Shares 'mod' with 'moderate' — keeps things measured, never over the top.

words.definition: Sullen, bad-tempered, and gloomy.
words.example: He sat morose in the corner, refusing to speak or join the celebration.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'more woes' — someone piling on more and more sorrow.

words.definition: Calmly relaxed and unconcerned, showing no worry or excitement.
words.example: She gave a nonchalant wave, as though nearly missing the flight meant nothing at all.
words.mnemonic: French 'non' (not) + 'chaloir' (to be warm/to care) — literally not heated up about anything.

words.definition: Refusing to change your mind or actions despite good reasons to do so.
words.example: The obstinate toddler clamped his mouth shut and would not try a single vegetable.
words.mnemonic: OB-STIN-ate sounds like 'ob-STAIN' — a stain that won't wash out no matter how hard you scrub.

words.definition: Too eager to give advice or use small authority in an interfering, unwelcome way.
words.example: An officious clerk insisted on inspecting every bag though no one had asked him to.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'office' — picture the bossy little office manager meddling in everyone's business.

words.definition: Holding firm views and stating them forcefully, often unwilling to accept other perspectives.
words.example: So opinionated was my uncle that dinner became a lecture on politics he refused to end.
words.mnemonic: Opinion + -ated: someone so full of opinions they're practically 'operated' by them.

words.definition: Deep in serious or wistful thought, often tinged with a touch of sadness.
words.example: She grew pensive by the window, staring at the rain and saying nothing for an hour.
words.mnemonic: PENSIVE echoes French 'penser' (to think) — a poet chewing a PEN, lost in thought.

words.definition: Deliberately breaking trust or betraying someone who relied on your loyalty.
words.example: The perfidious advisor smiled at the king by day and sold his secrets by night.
words.mnemonic: PER-FID-ious: 'fid' from Latin fides (faith), 'per-' meaning away from — faith cast away.

words.definition: Holding firmly and persistently to a purpose despite difficulty or opposition.
words.example: The pertinacious reporter phoned the senator every day for months until she finally answered.
words.mnemonic: 'per-' (through) + Latin 'tenax' (holding) — like a pit bull that clamps down and won't let go.

words.definition: Having a calm, unemotional temperament that stays unruffled even under pressure.
words.example: While others panicked at the alarm, the phlegmatic captain calmly finished his coffee.
words.mnemonic: From 'phlegm', the sluggish body humor — imagine someone too laid-back to react to anything.

words.definition: Calm and peaceful, with little movement or disturbance.
words.example: The placid lake mirrored the mountains without a single ripple at dawn.
words.mnemonic: PLACID sounds like 'please, sit' — a restful, unhurried scene where everyone settles down.

words.definition: Showing an inflated sense of self-importance through grand words or manner.
words.example: The pompous host reminded guests three times that his wine cost more than their cars.
words.mnemonic: POMPous is full of 'pomp' — picture a strutting peacock puffed up with pride.

words.definition: Spending money or resources freely and wastefully, with no care for the future.
words.example: His prodigal spending on parties emptied the fortune his grandfather spent a lifetime building.
words.mnemonic: Recall the biblical 'Prodigal Son' who blew his whole inheritance — recklessly wasteful.

words.definition: Recklessly wasteful with resources, and often shamelessly immoral in behavior.
words.example: The profligate heir gambled away the estate and drank through what little remained.
words.mnemonic: PRO-FLIG-ate: 'pro-' + 'fling it' — imagine flinging money away while living loosely.

words.definition: Showing careful, sensible judgment and thinking ahead to avoid needless risk.
words.example: It was prudent of her to save six months' salary before quitting to start a business.
words.mnemonic: PRUDENT sounds like 'prude' — a cautious, careful person who avoids anything risky.

words.definition: Complaining in a whining, peevish, and irritable manner.
words.example: The querulous passenger griped about the seat, the food, and the temperature all flight long.
words.mnemonic: QUERULOUS holds 'quer-' like 'query' — someone forever querying and grumbling in a whiny voice.

words.definition: Full of bitter, long-lasting resentment or ill will toward someone.
words.example: Their rancorous divorce dragged on for years, each accusing the other in open court.
words.mnemonic: RANCOROUS sounds like 'rank' + 'sour' — a rank, sour bitterness festering inside.

words.definition: Acting too hastily and without thinking about the consequences.
words.example: Quitting his job in anger was a rash decision he regretted the very next morning.
words.mnemonic: A skin RASH erupts suddenly without warning — a rash act happens suddenly without thinking.
